title: Infectious Skin Diseases
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)

overview.intro: This chapter explains the infections and infection-linked reactions of the skin: bacterial, fungal, viral, mycobacterial, toxin mediated, and parasitic. The organizing idea is depth and barrier. Each organism reaches a particular layer, and the layer it reaches sets the appearance of the lesion, the organism you should name, and the complication that follows. Board questions give a setting (a child with crusted lesions, a wrestler with recurrent abscesses, a gardener pricked by a thorn) and ask for the organism, its virulence factor, the histologic level of the split, or the sequela to expect. Work from exposure to barrier breach to layer involved, and most of these questions answer themselves.

connections.how: Every infection in this chapter begins with a breach in the stratum corneum or a follicular opening, so the barrier defenses determine who gets infected and how deeply.

The pattern of skin infection reports the arm of immunity that failed: Th17 defects give chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, T cell defects give extensive warts and molluscum, and neutrophil defects give recurrent abscesses.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows impetigo as well as pharyngitis, so a skin infection can present weeks later as hematuria.
Staphylococcal exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1, the same target as the autoantibody of pemphigus foliaceus, so toxin and autoimmunity produce the same split level.
Tetanospasmin, herpes zoster latency in the dorsal root ganglion, and leprous nerve damage all enter through the skin and act on the nervous system.

sections.title: Acne vulgaris: four steps in the pilosebaceous unit

blocks.text: Acne is a disease of the pilosebaceous unit: a hair follicle, its sebaceous gland, and the short duct joining them. The unit is dense on the face, chest, upper back, and shoulders, which is exactly where acne appears. Sebaceous glands are holocrine, meaning the whole cell disintegrates to release sebum, a mixture of triglycerides, wax esters, and squalene. Gland size and sebum output are under androgen control, which is why acne begins at adrenarche and puberty and why it tracks androgen excess at any age.

Four events must combine, and no single one produces the disease. First, keratinocytes lining the follicular infundibulum proliferate and fail to shed, so corneocytes stay stuck together and obstruct the duct; this microcomedone is the invisible primary lesion. Second, androgens, with testosterone converted to the more potent dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha reductase in the gland, enlarge the gland and raise sebum output, so material accumulates behind the plug. Third, the sealed, lipid rich, oxygen poor follicle is an ideal niche for Cutibacterium acnes, an anaerobic gram positive commensal rod whose density rises sharply inside the comedone. Fourth, inflammation follows: bacterial lipases release irritating free fatty acids from sebum triglycerides, bacterial components signal through toll-like receptor 2 to release interleukin 1 beta, interleukin 8, and tumor necrosis factor alpha, and neutrophils arrive.

blocks.text: The lesion type reports how far the sequence has gone. Comedones are noninflamed plugs, while rupture of the distended follicle spills keratin, sebum, and bacteria into the dermis, where they behave as foreign material; superficial rupture gives an inflamed papule or pustule and deep rupture a tender nodule or draining sinus. Because nodular lesions destroy dermal collagen and the follicle itself, they heal with atrophic or hypertrophic scars, while comedones do not scar.

blocks.text: Anything that raises androgen effect or follicular keratinization aggravates acne. Polycystic ovary syndrome raises ovarian androgen output and lowers sex hormone binding globulin, so free testosterone rises and acne appears with hirsutism and irregular cycles; congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen secreting tumors do the same more abruptly. Glucocorticoids, endogenous in Cushing syndrome or exogenous, produce a monomorphic eruption of follicular papules and pustules, often truncal and lacking comedones, reflecting direct steroid induced follicular inflammation rather than the full four step sequence. Acne beginning abruptly in an adult woman, or with virilization, points to an androgen source needing evaluation.

blocks.predict: A 23 year old woman has new jawline acne with hirsutism and cycles every 45 days. Which of the four steps is being driven, and why does free androgen rise more than total testosterone suggests?
blocks.explain: The androgen driven sebum step. In polycystic ovary syndrome, hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian androgen production and suppresses hepatic sex hormone binding globulin, so more of the total testosterone circulates free and reaches the 5-alpha reductase of the gland.

sections.title: Cutaneous and mucosal candidiasis

blocks.text: Candida albicans is a dimorphic commensal yeast of the gastrointestinal tract, mouth, and vagina that becomes pathogenic when the environment or the host changes. It is not a dermatophyte and does not digest keratin; it needs moisture, warmth, and a macerated or breached stratum corneum. That requirement explains the distribution. Candidal intertrigo occupies the skin folds, where apposed surfaces trap sweat, raise local pH, and soften the barrier: the inguinal and gluteal creases, axillae, inframammary folds, abdominal pannus, interdigital web spaces, and the angles of the mouth. The plaque is described as beefy red, moist, and sharply bordered with a fringe of loose scale, and the finding that makes the diagnosis is a ring of small satellite pustules just beyond the plaque edge, produced as yeast spreads onto adjacent skin.

In the diaper area this anatomy separates two diseases. Candidal diaper dermatitis involves the depths of the inguinal and gluteal folds, because that is where moisture collects, and it carries satellite pustules. Irritant (contact) diaper dermatitis is caused by urine, feces, fecal proteases and lipases, and friction acting on skin that touches the diaper, so it involves the convex surfaces of the buttocks, lower abdomen, and thighs and characteristically spares the creases, which the diaper does not contact. Candidal involvement often follows irritant dermatitis, since a damaged barrier invites colonizing yeast.

blocks.text: On mucosa the same organism produces thrush: adherent white plaques on the buccal mucosa, palate, and tongue that scrape off to leave an erythematous, sometimes bleeding base, which distinguishes them from the fixed white plaques of leukoplakia or oral hairy leukoplakia. Scraping a lesion and treating it with potassium hydroxide shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae; germ tube formation in serum is the classic identifying feature of C albicans in the laboratory.

Because Candida is already present, candidiasis is a report on host defense. Neutrophils and macrophages handle invasive candidiasis, while mucosal and cutaneous control depends on Th17 cells and interleukin 17, which drive epithelial antimicrobial peptide production and neutrophil recruitment. Defects along the interleukin 17 axis, including autosomal dominant hyper IgE (STAT3) syndrome, STAT1 gain of function mutations, and autoimmune polyendocrinopathy with autoantibodies to interleukin 17, produce chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis: persistent, recurring, treatment resistant candidal infection of skin, nails, and mucosa without disseminated disease. Thrush in an adult who has no local explanation, or esophageal candidiasis, points to T cell deficiency, most importantly advanced HIV infection.

sections.title: Erysipelas versus cellulitis: depth sets the border

blocks.text: Erysipelas and cellulitis are both spreading bacterial infections of the skin, and the single fact that organizes every difference between them is the depth of tissue involved. Erysipelas occupies the upper dermis and the superficial dermal lymphatics. Because the dermis is a dense, relatively confined compartment and because infection travels along discrete lymphatic channels, the edematous inflamed tissue is elevated above the surrounding skin and its edge is sharply demarcated, so the border can be traced with a pen. The plaque is bright red, hot, tense, and tender, classically on the face in a butterfly distribution or on the lower leg, and systemic symptoms (abrupt fever, chills) often precede the skin findings by hours. Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus) is the usual organism, with other beta hemolytic streptococci next.

Cellulitis involves the deep dermis and the subcutaneous fat. The hypodermis is a loose, septate, fatty compartment through which edema diffuses without boundary, so cellulitis is warm, red, swollen, and tender with borders that fade gradually into normal skin and cannot be outlined. It is deeper and flatter, less often elevated, and usually more indolent in onset. Both S pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus cause cellulitis, with staphylococci favored when there is a focal purulent center, an abscess, or a penetrating wound, and streptococci favored in diffuse nonpurulent disease.

blocks.caption: A tissue plane difference produces every clinical difference, including which organism is more likely.

blocks.text: Neither infection occurs through intact skin, so the portal of entry is part of the diagnosis and is where board questions hide the answer. Interdigital fissures from tinea pedis are the classic portal for recurrent leg cellulitis, and the bacterial episodes keep recurring for as long as that fissure stays open. Other portals are traumatic wounds and surgical incisions, venous stasis and diabetic ulcers, insect and animal bites, intravenous catheter sites and injection drug use, eczema or psoriasis with excoriation, and toe web maceration. Anything that impairs lymphatic drainage, including prior erysipelas, lymph node dissection, chronic lymphedema, and venous insufficiency, both predisposes to infection and is made worse by it: each episode scars lymphatics, raises local protein rich edema, and sets up the next episode.

blocks.caption: Each episode damages the drainage that would have prevented it, which is why recurrence clusters in one limb.

blocks.text: Streptococcus pyogenes spreads through tissue rather than forming abscesses because of its enzymes: hyaluronidase degrades the hyaluronic acid of the dermal matrix, streptokinase dissolves fibrin that would wall off the infection, and DNases break down the neutrophil extracellular traps that bind bacteria. Its M protein resists phagocytosis and binds fibrinogen, and its hyaluronic acid capsule mimics host matrix. Staphylococcus aureus, by contrast, makes coagulase and clumping factor, which promote local fibrin deposition and walling off, which is the mechanistic reason staphylococcal skin infection tends toward discrete abscesses while streptococcal infection spreads diffusely.

sections.title: Complications of cellulitis, including necrotizing fasciitis

blocks.text: Cellulitis can extend in three directions, and each gives a recognizable complication. Extending and coalescing, it liquefies tissue into an abscess: a fluctuant collection of neutrophils, necrotic debris, and organisms, usually Staphylococcus aureus, walled off by granulation tissue. Because an avascular pus filled cavity is cut off from circulating defenses and its acidic, hypoxic interior impairs neutrophil killing, the collection persists on its own, so cellulitis that does not resolve raises the question of an occult abscess. Extending along dermal lymphatics it produces lymphangitis, with tender red streaks running proximally and node tenderness. Extending into vessels it produces bacteremia, with fever, rigors, and risk of seeding endocarditis, vertebral osteomyelitis, or septic arthritis, and in severe disease the superantigen mediated toxic shock syndromes.

The complication that must be recognized immediately is necrotizing fasciitis, which spreads along the superficial fascia rather than through fat. Fascial planes are avascular, loose, and continuous over long distances, so organisms and toxins travel rapidly with little resistance. The infection thromboses the perforating vessels that cross the fascia to supply the overlying skin and the nerves running with them, and two consequences follow directly. Deep tissue is dying while the surface still looks mildly involved, so pain is out of proportion to the physical findings, the single most useful early clue. Then, as cutaneous nerves infarct, the excruciating area becomes anesthetic, and skin that was red turns dusky, then bullous, then frankly necrotic.

blocks.text: Two forms are distinguished. Type I is polymicrobial, mixing aerobes with anaerobes, and arises in older adults with diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, or recent abdominal or perineal surgery; Fournier gangrene of the perineum is this form. Type II is monomicrobial Streptococcus pyogenes, sometimes with S aureus, and can strike healthy young people after minor trauma, often with streptococcal toxic shock from superantigen release. Crepitus and gas on imaging mean gas forming organisms, classically Clostridium perfringens or mixed anaerobes. Laboratory clues reflect tissue destruction rather than the organism: marked leukocytosis with a left shift, creatine kinase release from involved muscle, hyponatremia, acidosis, and a rising lactate.

blocks.title: Worked example: two red legs
blocks.text: Patient A has a hot, bright red, sharply bordered plaque on the shin, fever of 38.6 C (101.5 F), and tenderness that matches the redness. Patient B has a dull red, slightly swollen thigh, pain scored 10 of 10 that required escalating analgesia overnight, a heart rate of 130, blood pressure of 85 over 50, and a patch that is now numb to light touch. Patient A has erysipelas: the sharp raised border places the infection in the upper dermis, and pain proportional to findings means the process is where it looks. Patient B has necrotizing fasciitis: pain and shock exceeding visible disease, with developing anesthesia, indicate fascial spread with thrombosis of perforating vessels and cutaneous nerves, so the surface understates what has died beneath it.

sections.title: Erythema nodosum as septal panniculitis

blocks.text: Erythema nodosum is not an infection of the skin; it is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction in subcutaneous fat to an antigen located elsewhere. Subcutaneous fat is organized into lobules of adipocytes separated by fibrous septa that carry the arterioles, venules, and lymphatics supplying the fat. Inflammation confined to those septa is a septal panniculitis, and erythema nodosum is the prototype. Early lesions show neutrophils and edema in widened septa; established lesions show lymphocytes, histiocytes, and small histiocytic granulomas within the widened septa. Critically, there is no vasculitis: vessel walls are not destroyed by fibrinoid necrosis, and the fat lobules themselves are spared.

That histology predicts the clinical picture exactly. Because the inflammation is deep, the lesions are palpable nodules felt more easily than seen, with ill defined edges and overlying erythema rather than a sharp epidermal border. Because septal vessels are inflamed but not necrosed and the lobules survive, the lesions do not ulcerate, do not suppurate, and resolve over two to eight weeks like a deep bruise, leaving transient yellow brown discoloration but no scar and no atrophy. They are strikingly tender and warm, usually 1 to 5 cm, bilateral, and distributed over the pretibial surface of the shins, where fat is thin over bone and septal anatomy is prominent. Fever, malaise, and arthralgias commonly accompany the eruption.

blocks.caption: A nodule on the shin that ulcerates or scars is not erythema nodosum, and that single observation redirects the differential.

blocks.text: The value of recognizing erythema nodosum is that it is a signal of something systemic. The antigen may be microbial, from a granulomatous disease, from bowel inflammation, or hormonal. Streptococcal pharyngitis is the most common identifiable trigger overall, particularly in children, with the eruption appearing two to three weeks after the sore throat. In regions where they are endemic, coccidioidomycosis and histoplasmosis are frequent causes, and in coccidioidomycosis erythema nodosum actually marks a vigorous cell mediated response and a favorable prognosis. Sarcoidosis is a major cause, and the combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever, and arthritis is named Lofgren syndrome. Tuberculosis, inflammatory bowel disease (both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, often tracking bowel activity), pregnancy and exogenous estrogen or progestin, Yersinia and other enteric infections, and Behcet disease round out the list; a substantial fraction remains idiopathic.

sections.title: Folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, and abscesses

blocks.text: The follicular ostium is a funnel of epidermis that opens the barrier, and Staphylococcus aureus, which colonizes the anterior nares and moist skin of a large minority of people, enters through it. The resulting lesions form one family graded only by depth and lateral extent, so the naming follows the anatomy. Folliculitis is suppuration confined to the ostium and upper follicle: small dome shaped pustules each pierced by a hair, superficial and nonscarring. A furuncle (boil) occurs when infection penetrates the full length of the follicle into dermis and subcutaneous tissue, forming a deep tender fluctuant nodule that points and drains a necrotic core, and because the follicle is destroyed it can scar. A carbuncle is several adjacent furuncles coalescing into one indurated plaque draining through multiple ostia, typically on the thick skin of the posterior neck, upper back, or thighs, with fever and malaise because the tissue volume involved is large.

blocks.caption: One organism and one anatomic route produce three named lesions; only the depth and number of follicles differ.

blocks.text: Related suppurative lesions sit outside the follicle but behave the same way. A cutaneous abscess is a walled off collection of pus in the dermis and deeper tissue, most often from S aureus, arising from an infected follicle, a puncture, or an inoculated foreign body; it is fluctuant, exquisitely tender, and persists on its own because the avascular, acidic, hypoxic cavity is cut off from circulating defenses and does not support neutrophil killing. A pilonidal abscess arises in the sacrococcygeal cleft, where hair fragments are driven into the midline skin by friction and sitting; the hairs act as a foreign body and a conduit, a sinus forms, and the cavity becomes infected with skin and enteric flora. Hidradenitis suppurativa produces recurrent painful nodules, sinus tracts, and scarring in the axillae and groin and is primarily a disease of follicular occlusion rather than a primary infection, which is why it recurs despite drainage.

blocks.text: Exposure can override the usual organism. Hot tub folliculitis follows immersion in inadequately chlorinated hot tubs and whirlpools; Pseudomonas aeruginosa tolerates warm water in which chlorine dissipates, and swimsuit occlusion macerates the stratum corneum, so itchy follicular pustules appear one to two days later in the distribution the suit covered and are usually self limited. Gram negative folliculitis of the face follows prolonged antibiotic suppression of normal flora, and Malassezia folliculitis gives monomorphic itchy truncal papules in humid conditions. Host factors matter as well: diabetes, obesity with intertriginous friction, nasal carriage of S aureus, and neutrophil disorders such as chronic granulomatous disease or leukocyte adhesion deficiency all produce recurrent furuncles, so recurrent abscesses in a child should prompt evaluation of neutrophil function.

sections.title: Nonbullous and bullous impetigo, and poststreptococcal sequelae

blocks.text: Impetigo is the most superficial bacterial skin infection, confined to the epidermis above the basal layer, which is why it heals without scarring. It is predominantly a disease of preschool and school age children, favored by warm humid weather, crowding, and any breach that lets surface flora in: insect bites, scratches, scabies, eczema, and varicella lesions. Two forms exist, and they are separated not by severity but by whether a toxin is involved.

Nonbullous impetigo accounts for the great majority. Bacteria colonize a minor abrasion, a vesicle or pustule forms and ruptures within hours, and the exuded serum and neutrophils dry into a thick adherent golden crust described as honey colored, classically around the nose and mouth and on exposed limbs. Lesions spread by autoinoculation from scratching, and regional lymphadenopathy is common while fever is not. Staphylococcus aureus is now the most frequent isolate in most settings, with Streptococcus pyogenes also common and often found alongside it.

Bullous impetigo is toxin mediated and caused by S aureus alone. Certain strains secrete exfoliative (epidermolytic) toxins A and B, serine proteases with a single substrate: desmoglein 1, the desmosomal cadherin holding keratinocytes together in the superficial epidermis. Cleaving it separates cells within the granular layer, so intact fluid filled bullae form very high in the epidermis. Their thin roofs rupture easily and leave a shiny, moist, varnished erosion with a collarette of scale. In bullous impetigo the toxin acts where it is made, so bullae are limited to infected skin; when it reaches the circulation from a distant focus it splits the epidermis everywhere, which is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Desmoglein 1 is largely replaced by desmoglein 3 in mucosa, which is why mucosa is spared.

blocks.text: The important sequela belongs to the streptococcal form. Nephritogenic M types of S pyogenes, including skin associated types, elicit antibodies whose immune complexes deposit in the glomerulus and activate complement, so about three to six weeks after impetigo, a longer latency than the one to two weeks that follows pharyngitis, a child develops acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: cola colored urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, a low serum C3, and subepithelial humps on electron microscopy. Antistreptolysin O titers rise poorly after skin infection because skin lipids inhibit streptolysin O, so anti DNase B is the more useful marker. Acute rheumatic fever, in contrast, follows pharyngeal infection and has not been shown to follow impetigo, a distinction examiners test directly.

blocks.explain: No to both. Skin lipids inhibit streptolysin O, so anti DNase B is the better serologic marker after impetigo, and acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngeal, not cutaneous, streptococcal infection. Glomerulonephritis can follow either site.

sections.title: MRSA: mecA, SCCmec, and two epidemiologic patterns

blocks.text: Beta-lactam antibiotics work by binding the transpeptidase domain of penicillin binding proteins, the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan, so the wall cannot be completed and the dividing cell lyses. Staphylococcus aureus acquired two successive defenses. Penicillinase (a beta-lactamase) hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring and defeats penicillin, which is why penicillins carrying a bulky side chain that the enzyme cannot reach remain active. Methicillin resistance is a different and more complete mechanism: the organism acquires mecA, a gene encoding PBP2a, an alternative penicillin binding protein whose active site has very low affinity for essentially all beta-lactams. Wall synthesis therefore continues while the drug is present, so resistance extends to the entire beta-lactam class rather than to one agent.

mecA does not sit on the native chromosome. It is carried on the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec), a mobile genomic island integrated at a fixed site near the origin of replication and mobilized by its own recombinase genes. SCCmec types differ in size and content, and this difference underlies the two clinical patterns. The large types (I, II, III) found in healthcare associated strains carry additional resistance determinants, so hospital associated MRSA is typically resistant to multiple non beta-lactam classes as well. The small types (IV, V) carried by community strains impose less fitness cost and transfer more readily, so community strains spread efficiently among healthy people while remaining susceptible to several non beta-lactam agents.

blocks.text: Community acquired MRSA has a distinct virulence profile. Most strains carry Panton-Valentine leukocidin, a two component pore forming toxin that inserts into neutrophil and monocyte membranes and lyses them. Loss of the cells that would contain the infection explains the lesions: recurrent furuncles and spontaneous abscesses with central necrosis in people with no healthcare exposure, and in a minority a severe necrotizing pneumonia, often following influenza. Transmission requires skin contact or shared items, so outbreaks cluster among contact athletes, military recruits, correctional and child care facilities, households, and people who inject drugs. Healthcare associated MRSA instead reflects selection pressure and devices: recent hospitalization or surgery, indwelling catheters and prosthetic material, hemodialysis, long term care, and prolonged antibiotic exposure, with bacteremia, surgical site infection, and ventilator associated pneumonia rather than isolated boils.

blocks.text: Reservoir matters as much as resistance. Roughly a quarter to a third of people carry S aureus in the anterior nares at any time, where it adheres to squamous epithelium through wall teichoic acid and clumping factor B. Carriers autoinoculate breaks in their own skin, which is why one patient has repeated boils with an identical strain, and they shed organisms to others, so the nares rather than the lesion is the reservoir that sustains recurrent disease and perioperative transmission. The laboratory detects resistance using cefoxitin as a surrogate marker for mecA or by detecting mecA directly; S aureus itself is a catalase positive, coagulase positive, beta-hemolytic, mannitol fermenting gram positive coccus in clusters.

sections.title: Molluscum contagiosum

blocks.text: Molluscum contagiosum virus is a large double stranded DNA poxvirus that infects humans only and has no animal reservoir. Like all poxviruses it replicates entirely in the cytoplasm using its own transcription machinery, and it infects only keratinocytes. Infection is restricted to the epidermis, where it drives proliferation without inducing the destructive inflammation of a herpesvirus, so the lesion is a growth rather than a vesicle or ulcer.

The lesion is a firm, flesh colored to pearly, dome shaped papule, typically 2 to 5 mm, with a central dell or umbilication from which a white keratinous core can be expressed. Lesions are usually multiple, grouped where skin has been rubbed or scratched, and asymptomatic, although a surrounding eczematous reaction (molluscum dermatitis) may itch. Histology is distinctive and often tested: the epidermis forms a lobulated, cup shaped downgrowth into the dermis, and infected keratinocytes contain large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) that displace the nucleus; the central umbilication corresponds to the plugged opening of that crater.

blocks.text: Transmission requires direct contact with infected keratinocytes and occurs three ways. Skin to skin contact spreads it among children, in wrestling and gymnastics, and through shared towels or mats; autoinoculation by scratching explains linear or clustered lesions and spread to adjacent sites; and sexual contact explains lesions confined to the genitals, lower abdomen, and inner thighs in adults, which is why genital molluscum in an adult is treated as a sexually transmitted infection and why the finding in a child prompts careful but neutral consideration of how contact occurred. Incubation is roughly two weeks to six months.

Course is determined by cell mediated immunity. In an immunocompetent child the virus is eventually recognized and cleared, often after a period of lesion inflammation and redness that precedes resolution, so lesions are self limited over months up to about two years and heal without scarring unless traumatized or secondarily infected. With impaired T cell function the same virus produces far more and far larger lesions: in advanced HIV infection, particularly with low CD4 counts, molluscum becomes extensive and facial, with giant lesions exceeding 1 cm that are difficult to clear, and widespread molluscum in an adult is an indication to test for HIV. Lesions also become numerous where the barrier and local immunity are altered, as in atopic dermatitis and in skin under topical steroids.

sections.title: Dermatophytosis by site, and why tinea versicolor is different

blocks.text: Dermatophytes are keratinophilic molds of three genera, Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton, that secrete keratinases and therefore live only in dead keratinized tissue: the stratum corneum, the hair shaft, and the nail plate. They do not invade living epidermis or dermis in a normal host, which explains both the superficial scaling of the lesions and the fact that most of the inflammation is a host response to fungal antigen diffusing inward rather than to tissue invasion. On the trunk this produces the classic configuration: the fungus advances outward through the stratum corneum while the immune response clears the older central zone, leaving an annular plaque with a raised, scaly, sometimes vesicular active border and relative central clearing. Scale scraped from that advancing border, dissolved in potassium hydroxide, shows branching septate hyphae, and hyphae fluoresce with a chitin binding stain.

blocks.text: Two site specific points carry mechanism. Tinea cruris spares the scrotum while candidal intertrigo of the groin involves it, because dermatophytes need keratinized skin and thin, sebum rich scrotal skin is a poor substrate, whereas Candida thrives on moist apposed surfaces. Tinea capitis matters because the organism occupies the hair shaft: endothrix invasion breaks hairs at the surface leaving black dots, ectothrix invasion breaks them a few millimeters out, and a vigorous host response produces a kerion, which is sterile pus from immune attack on the fungus rather than bacterial superinfection. Because the fungus lies inside the hair shaft and the nail plate rather than on the surface, scalp and nail disease persist far longer than body disease.

Tinea versicolor is named by tradition rather than by cause. It is produced by Malassezia species, lipophilic commensal yeasts of sebaceous follicles that lack fatty acid synthase and so depend on sebum rather than on keratin; they are not dermatophytes. In hot humid conditions and on sebum rich skin the organism converts to a mycelial form and proliferates in the stratum corneum of the upper trunk, neck, and shoulders, producing well demarcated macules with fine branny scale. The macules may be lighter or darker than surrounding skin because Malassezia produces dicarboxylic acids, chiefly azelaic acid, that inhibit tyrosinase in melanocytes, so pigmentation falls in affected areas and the contrast becomes obvious after sun exposure tans the surrounding skin. Potassium hydroxide preparation shows the spaghetti and meatballs pattern of short hyphae with clusters of round yeast, which distinguishes it at a glance from the long branching hyphae of a dermatophyte.

sections.title: Human papillomavirus warts and their histology

blocks.text: Human papillomaviruses are small nonenveloped double stranded DNA viruses that infect basal keratinocytes reached through a microabrasion. The viral life cycle is tied to epithelial maturation: the episomal genome is maintained at low copy number in the dividing basal layer, early genes drive proliferation as the cell moves upward, and the capsid proteins L1 and L2 are expressed only in the uppermost differentiated layers, where fully assembled virions are shed in desquamating squames. The virus therefore never lyses a cell, causes no viremia, and presents little antigen to the immune system, which is why warts persist for months to years and why clearance, when it comes, depends on a cell mediated response.

Clinical type reflects anatomy and HPV type. Verruca vulgaris, the common wart, is a firm hyperkeratotic papule with a rough papillated surface on the hands, fingers, and periungual skin, and the thrombosed dermal capillaries at its tips appear as the black dots that distinguish it from a callus. Verruca plantaris, the plantar wart, is pressed inward by weight bearing into a flat, tender, keratotic plaque that interrupts the skin lines, separating it from a corn. Verruca plana, the flat wart, is a smooth, slightly elevated, skin colored papule in clusters on the face, dorsal hands, and shins, where linear arrays betray autoinoculation by shaving. Condyloma acuminatum, the anogenital wart, is a soft, moist, cauliflower like exophytic growth of the vulva, penis, perineum, and perianal skin, and about 90 percent are caused by the low risk types HPV 6 and 11, which do not integrate and rarely progress to cancer. The high risk types, chiefly HPV 16 and 18, integrate their genome, overexpress E6 and E7, which degrade p53 and inactivate the retinoblastoma protein, and cause squamous dysplasia and carcinoma rather than ordinary warts.

blocks.text: Histology is diagnostic and follows directly from the life cycle. Driving keratinocyte proliferation produces acanthosis (thickened epidermis) and papillomatosis (the epidermis thrown into finger like projections over dermal papillae containing dilated capillaries), with overlying hyperkeratosis and often parakeratosis. The hallmark cytopathic change is the koilocyte: a squamous cell of the upper layers with a shrunken, wrinkled, hyperchromatic nucleus surrounded by a clear perinuclear halo produced by collapse of the cytokeratin cytoskeleton, usually accompanied by coarse keratohyalin granules. Inward curving of the epidermal rete at the margins of the lesion completes the picture.

Because clearance requires T cell mediated recognition of infected keratinocytes rather than antibody, impaired cellular immunity produces extensive, confluent, and treatment refractory warts. This is seen in advanced HIV infection, in organ transplant recipients, in combined and T cell immunodeficiencies, and in two single gene diseases: epidermodysplasia verruciformis, in which EVER1 or EVER2 (TMC6, TMC8) mutations permit widespread infection by otherwise harmless beta HPV types with later squamous cell carcinoma on sun exposed skin, and WHIM syndrome, caused by gain of function CXCR4 mutations, whose acronym names warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections, and myelokathexis. Extensive warts are therefore a reason to evaluate T cell function.

sections.title: Bloodborne pathogen risk after a needle stick

blocks.text: A percutaneous needle injury inoculates a small volume of blood under the skin, so the probability that infection follows is governed by how much infectious virus that volume contains and how efficiently that virus establishes infection. The three pathogens of concern rank in a fixed order that tracks circulating titer. Hepatitis B virus circulates at very high levels in untreated chronic infection, often 100 million to a billion virions per milliliter, and has a very low infectious dose, giving a risk of about 30 percent from a hepatitis B e antigen positive source and about 1 to 6 percent when the source is e antigen negative, which marks lower replication. Hepatitis C circulates at intermediate titers and carries a risk of about 1.8 percent, usually rounded to 2 percent. HIV circulates at the lowest titers in untreated infection and is a fragile enveloped virus, giving about 0.3 percent after a percutaneous injury and about 0.09 percent after a mucous membrane splash.

blocks.text: Four features of the injury modify that baseline, and all four work through inoculum volume or through viral load. A hollow-bore needle, especially one used for venipuncture or arterial sampling, carries residual blood inside its lumen, so it delivers far more blood than a solid suture needle or scalpel edge, which carries only a surface film; this is the single most important device factor. A deep puncture deposits that blood into vascularized tissue instead of the superficial dermis. Visible blood on the device, and a needle taken directly from the source patient's vein or artery, both indicate fresh, undiluted blood. A high source viral load raises the number of infectious particles per unit volume, which is why a source with untreated acute or advanced HIV infection, or a hepatitis B e antigen positive source, carries much greater risk than a source with suppressed or low level viremia; conversely, a source on effective therapy with undetectable virus transmits far less efficiently.

blocks.text: Recipient factors complete the picture. Hepatitis B is the one of the three with an effective vaccine, and a documented anti-HBs response of at least 10 milli-international units per milliliter makes transmission very unlikely, so the highest risk pathogen is also the one whose outcome depends most on the recipient's prior immunity. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C or HIV. Intact skin is an effective barrier, so a splash onto unbroken skin carries negligible risk, while exposure of mucous membranes or nonintact skin is measurable but lower risk than a percutaneous injury.

sections.title: Predicting the organism from the wound exposure

blocks.text: Wound infections are inoculations: the organism comes from the flora of whatever broke the skin or from the environment the wound met, so an exposure in a question is asking for an organism. Dog and cat bites inoculate oral flora, in which Pasteurella multocida is prominent. Cat teeth are slender and drive bacteria deep into joints and tendon sheaths through a small wound, and Pasteurella divides rapidly, so cellulitis already intense within 12 to 24 hours is its signature, unlike the slower staphylococcal or streptococcal infection of two to three days. Capnocytophaga canimorsus, also from canine saliva, is cleared by splenic macrophages and opsonizing antibody, so in an asplenic or cirrhotic patient it causes fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans from a trivial bite.

Human bites and clenched fist injuries inoculate human oral flora, including Eikenella corrodens, a fastidious gram negative rod. The clenched fist injury over the metacarpophalangeal joint is dangerous out of proportion to its size because the extensor tendon and joint capsule are inoculated while the fist is closed, and when the hand opens the tendon slides proximally, carrying contamination into deep spaces no longer reachable from the surface.

Water exposure splits by salinity and temperature. Vibrio vulnificus is a halophilic gram negative rod of warm brackish and coastal water acquired through a seawater exposed wound or raw oysters. Its growth is iron dependent, so iron overload states and chronic liver disease, where transferrin saturation is high and macrophage function impaired, permit rapid bacteremia with hemorrhagic bullae and necrotizing fasciitis, while a healthy host usually has only gastroenteritis or local infection. Mycobacterium marinum is a slow growing nontuberculous mycobacterium of fresh and salt water that grows best at about 30 C (86 F), well below core temperature, so it causes indolent granulomatous nodules on the cooler hands and forearms of people who clean fish tanks, sometimes ascending the lymphatics, and its culture must be requested at low temperature or it will be missed.

Plant and soil exposures give Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus on rose thorns, sphagnum moss, hay, and soil. Inoculated by a thorn prick, it forms a painless papule or ulcer at the puncture site, then spreads up the draining lymphatic as a chain of subcutaneous nodules that ulcerate in sequence, the lymphocutaneous or sporotrichoid pattern. It grows as a mold in the environment and as cigar shaped budding yeast in tissue at 37 C (98.6 F).

sections.title: Clostridial wound disease: gas gangrene and tetanus

blocks.text: Clostridia are anaerobic, spore forming, gram positive rods of soil and of the human colon. Spores germinate only where the redox potential is low, so clostridial disease requires a wound that excludes oxygen: crushed devitalized muscle, a deep puncture that closes over itself, a wound contaminated with soil or feces, or ischemic tissue. The two diseases that follow are purely toxin mediated, and the toxins act in different compartments, which is why one destroys tissue locally and the other leaves the wound unimpressive while paralyzing the patient.

Clostridium perfringens causes clostridial myonecrosis, or gas gangrene. Its principal virulence factor is alpha toxin, a phospholipase C also called lecithinase, which hydrolyzes lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) and sphingomyelin in cell membranes. Lysing the membranes of myocytes, endothelium, erythrocytes, platelets, and leukocytes produces immediate myonecrosis, intravascular hemolysis, microvascular thrombosis, and destruction of the neutrophils that would contain the infection. Thrombosis extends the anaerobic zone, so the organism creates its own habitat and advances rapidly, while fermentation of muscle glycogen releases gas into tissue and produces crepitus. Clinically there is severe pain, tense edema, thin brown malodorous discharge, dusky skin, hemolysis with hemoglobinuria, and strikingly few neutrophils on Gram stain of an exudate full of large gram positive rods. The laboratory shows a double zone of hemolysis on blood agar and a positive lecithinase (Nagler) reaction on egg yolk agar.

blocks.text: Clostridium tetani does the opposite: it remains confined to a wound, a splinter, nail puncture, burn, or neonatal umbilical stump, and causes little local inflammation. Its toxin, tetanospasmin, is a zinc dependent metalloprotease cleaved into a heavy chain that binds and delivers and a light chain that cuts. The heavy chain binds gangliosides at the presynaptic membrane of the alpha motor neuron, and the internalized toxin travels by retrograde axonal transport to the anterior horn. Rather than acting there, it crosses the synapse into the terminals of the inhibitory interneurons of the spinal cord and brainstem, where the light chain cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP), a SNARE protein required for vesicle fusion, so glycine and GABA cannot be released.

Loss of inhibition, not stimulation, produces every sign of tetanus. Alpha motor neurons fire without restraint and reciprocal inhibition of antagonists fails, so muscles contract simultaneously and rigidly: trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonos, a board like abdomen, and laryngeal and respiratory spasm that causes death. The patient remains fully conscious and the spasms are exquisitely painful and triggered by minor stimuli, because sensory pathways are untouched, and loss of inhibition in preganglionic sympathetic neurons adds labile blood pressure, tachycardia, and sweating. Recovery requires growth of new nerve terminals, which is why tetanus lasts weeks. Botulinum toxin is the instructive contrast: the same class of SNARE cleaving metalloprotease, but acting peripherally on cholinergic terminals at the neuromuscular junction, so acetylcholine release fails and paralysis is flaccid and descending. The toxin class is identical; the synapse targeted decides whether the patient is stiff or limp.

sections.title: Herpes simplex and herpes zoster in the skin

blocks.text: Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 and varicella-zoster virus are enveloped double stranded DNA alphaherpesviruses sharing a two phase life history. Primary infection occurs in epithelium, where the virus replicates and lyses keratinocytes, and lysis with intraepidermal edema produces the intraepidermal vesicle. A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant keratinocytes with ballooning degeneration and intranuclear inclusions, which does not distinguish the three viruses. The virus then enters sensory nerve endings in the lesion, travels by retrograde axonal transport to the sensory ganglion, and establishes latency as an episome with minimal gene expression, invisible to cytotoxic T cells because almost no viral peptide reaches the cell surface. Reactivation sends virus anterograde down the same axon, which is why recurrences return to the territory of the latently infected neuron.

That rule explains the clinical patterns of herpes simplex. Herpes labialis recurs at the vermilion border because the trigeminal ganglion was seeded, and burning or tingling precedes it as virus travels down the nerve. Genital herpes, more often HSV-2, recurs in sacral dermatomes. Primary gingivostomatitis in a child is far more extensive than any recurrence, with fever, painful oral ulcers, and adenopathy, because no memory exists yet. Herpetic whitlow is inoculation of a finger, classically in dentists and thumb sucking children, giving deep painful vesicles mistaken for a bacterial felon. Eczema herpeticum occurs when HSV lands on skin whose barrier defenses are impaired by atopic dermatitis, so it disseminates across eczematous skin as monomorphic punched out erosions with fever.

Varicella-zoster virus follows the same rules with different geography. Primary infection is varicella, which is viremic and therefore seeds many sensory ganglia at once. Decades later, as virus specific T cell surveillance wanes with age, immunosuppression, or malignancy, the virus reactivates in a single ganglion and spreads down all the axons of that neuron population, producing herpes zoster: grouped vesicles on an erythematous base confined to one dermatome, stopping at the midline, usually thoracic or trigeminal, preceded for several days by pain or dysesthesia before any rash. Involvement of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve threatens the eye, and lesions on the nasal tip (the nasociliary branch) predict it. Reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve produces Ramsay Hunt syndrome: vesicles in the ear canal and on the auricle, ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy, and often vertigo and hearing loss, because that ganglion lies beside the facial motor fibers and the vestibulocochlear nerve. Lesions crossing dermatomes indicate immunosuppression.

blocks.text: Postherpetic neuralgia is the main sequela of zoster and follows neural injury rather than ongoing infection. Inflammation within the ganglion and nerve destroys neurons and produces fibrosis and demyelination, with preferential loss of large myelinated fibers; surviving small nociceptive fibers become spontaneously active and centrally sensitized, so pain persists after the rash heals. It is defined as dermatomal pain beyond about three months, often with allodynia, and its strongest risk factor is age, with incidence rising steeply after 60 years.

sections.title: Viral exanthems: measles, rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum

blocks.text: A viral exanthem is a rash produced by a systemic viral infection, and in most cases it is an immune response to virus in dermal capillaries rather than viral destruction of the epidermis. That is why these rashes are maculopapular rather than vesicular, why they appear several days into the illness as the adaptive response matures, and why their timing relative to fever is itself diagnostic.

Measles, caused by a negative sense RNA paramyxovirus, is the most severe of the four. About 10 days after exposure, a prodrome of high fever with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis reflects respiratory epithelial infection and viremia. Late in the prodrome, Koplik spots appear on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars as tiny blue white papules on a red base, an enanthem specific for measles that precedes the rash by a day or two. The exanthem begins behind the ears and at the hairline and spreads downward, becoming confluent, with fever peaking as the rash peaks, then fading in the same order with fine desquamation. Complications follow its suppression of lymphocyte function and its tropism: otitis media and bacterial pneumonia (the commonest cause of death), giant cell pneumonia in the immunocompromised, acute postinfectious encephalitis, and, years later, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

Rubella, caused by a positive sense RNA togavirus, is milder but has a more useful sign: tender postauricular, suboccipital, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy that often precedes and outlasts the rash. The exanthem is a fine pink maculopapular eruption that also begins on the face and spreads downward but never becomes confluent and clears in about three days, with arthralgias common in adolescent and adult women. Its importance lies in congenital rubella syndrome: first trimester infection crosses the placenta and causes sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and cardiac defects, most characteristically patent ductus arteriosus.

Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, sixth disease) is caused by human herpesvirus 6 and affects infants roughly 6 months to 2 years, the window after maternal antibody wanes. The pattern is three to five days of high fever, often 39.5 to 40.5 C (103 to 105 F), in a child who looks surprisingly well, and then, as the fever breaks, a rose pink macular rash on the trunk spreading to the neck and proximal limbs and sparing the face. Fever this high makes it the classic cause of a first febrile seizure, and the illness is otherwise benign.

Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is caused by parvovirus B19, a single stranded DNA virus that infects erythroid progenitors through the P antigen receptor and halts erythropoiesis. A mild febrile illness during viremia is followed, as antibody appears, by bright confluent erythema of both cheeks with circumoral pallor (slapped cheek) and then a reticulated lacy rash on the limbs and trunk that can recur for weeks with heat or sun. Because the rash is immune mediated and arrives after viremia, the child is typically no longer contagious once it is visible. The same arrest of erythropoiesis explains transient aplastic crisis in anyone dependent on rapid red cell turnover, chronic anemia in immunodeficiency, and hydrops fetalis after maternal infection.

sections.title: Varicella, enteroviral eruptions, and scarlet fever

blocks.text: Three more childhood eruptions are separated by the kind of lesion each produces, which in turn reflects what the organism does to the epidermis. Varicella and the enteroviral eruptions kill keratinocytes and therefore blister; scarlet fever is toxin mediated vasodilation and therefore produces erythema with a texture change but no vesicle.

Varicella (chickenpox) is primary infection with varicella-zoster virus, acquired by respiratory droplets and contact with vesicle fluid. The virus replicates in respiratory mucosa and regional nodes, and primary and secondary viremias carry it to the skin after about 14 days; because seeding occurs in successive waves, new lesions keep appearing for several days. That wave pattern produces the most useful finding: lesions in different stages side by side in the same area, macules, papules, clear vesicles, pustules, and crusts at once. The eruption is centripetal, beginning on the trunk, face, and scalp with mucosal involvement and fewer lesions distally, and is intensely pruritic. Lesions heal without scarring unless scratched and secondarily infected with S aureus or S pyogenes, the commonest complication. In adults and in immunocompromised or pregnant patients, varicella pneumonia and visceral dissemination make it far more severe, and the virus then lies latent in sensory ganglia. Smallpox is the contrast examiners use: deep umbilicated lesions, centrifugal distribution, and all lesions at the same stage, because seeding was synchronous.

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease and herpangina are caused by enteroviruses, principally coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71 for the former and coxsackievirus A for the latter: nonenveloped positive sense RNA viruses spread by the fecal-oral and respiratory routes, peaking in late summer. In hand-foot-and-mouth disease, fever and oral pain are followed by shallow painful ulcers of the anterior mouth and by oval gray vesicles on the palms, soles, and often buttocks, oriented along skin lines, with nail shedding sometimes weeks later. Herpangina gives abrupt fever with vesicles and ulcers restricted to the posterior pharynx, soft palate, and tonsillar pillars, sparing the anterior mouth, which separates it from hand-foot-and-mouth disease and from herpetic gingivostomatitis. Enterovirus 71 is associated with brainstem encephalitis and aseptic meningitis.

blocks.text: Scarlet fever is not a viral exanthem. It accompanies Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis in a patient lacking antibody to that strain's streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin. These exotoxins are superantigens: they bind simultaneously to the outside of the major histocompatibility complex class II molecule and to the variable region of the T cell receptor beta chain, bypassing antigen processing and activating a large fraction of T cells at once. The resulting flood of interleukin 1, interleukin 2, interferon gamma, and tumor necrosis factor produces fever, cutaneous vasodilation, and endothelial activation. One to two days after the sore throat, a fine blanching punctate erythema starts on the neck and upper trunk and spreads outward, and because each papule is centered on a follicle it feels like sandpaper, its most characteristic quality. Flexural accentuation gives linear petechial streaks (Pastia lines), the cheeks flush while perioral skin stays pale, and the tongue is first white coated with projecting inflamed papillae, then a beefy red strawberry tongue. The rash resolves with desquamation of the hands and feet one to two weeks later, and this illness, unlike the others here, carries risk of rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.

sections.title: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome versus toxic epidermal necrolysis

blocks.text: Two diseases make large sheets of epidermis separate, and they are distinguished by the level at which the epidermis splits and the mechanism that split it. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is toxin mediated separation high in a living epidermis; toxic epidermal necrolysis is immune mediated death of the entire epidermis. That difference determines the age group, mucosal involvement, the appearance of the denuded base, and how dangerous the illness is.

In staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, a focus of Staphylococcus aureus elsewhere than the skin that peels, often the nasopharynx, conjunctiva, umbilicus, or a minor wound, secretes exfoliative toxin A or B into the blood. The toxin cleaves desmoglein 1, so keratinocytes separate within the granular layer: they are not killed, they are unstuck. Fever and tender erythroderma are followed by flaccid bullae and sheets of epidermis sliding off with gentle lateral pressure (a positive Nikolsky sign), leaving a moist, bright red base. Because the split lies just beneath the stratum corneum, little tissue is lost and the base re-epithelializes from intact keratinocytes in one to two weeks without scarring. It occurs almost entirely in children under about 5 years, because renal clearance of the toxin is immature and antitoxin antibody has not developed, and mucosa is spared because desmoglein 3 compensates there. Blood cultures are usually negative, since the toxin acts at a distance, so the organism is cultured from the original focus.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis is a severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction, continuous with Stevens-Johnson syndrome and separated from it only by the surface area detached (under 10 percent there, over 30 percent here). A drug, most often a sulfonamide, an aromatic anticonvulsant such as carbamazepine or phenytoin, allopurinol, or a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent, generates a drug specific CD8 cytotoxic T cell response against keratinocytes; granulysin, perforin, and Fas ligand drive apoptosis, so the epidermis dies full thickness and separates at the dermoepidermal junction. Prodromal fever is followed by painful dusky macules with targetoid centers that coalesce, then detachment of gray full thickness epidermis, leaving a raw dermis. Two or more mucosal surfaces are involved in most cases: hemorrhagic crusting of the lips, conjunctivitis risking corneal scarring, and genital erosions. Losing the whole epidermis means losing the barrier, so fluid and protein loss, hypothermia, and sepsis follow as in a large burn, and mortality is high.

blocks.title: Worked example: two children with peeling skin
blocks.text: Child A is 3, febrile, with crusting around the nares, tender red skin, and flaccid blisters peeling from the neck and groin to leave a moist pink base; the mouth is normal. Child B is 11, began carbamazepine three weeks ago, and has dusky patches that became gray sheets lifting off the chest, with eroded crusted lips and conjunctivitis. Child A has staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: the nasal focus produces exfoliative toxin, desmoglein 1 is cleaved in the granular layer, and spared mucosa plus a superficial moist base confirm an intraepidermal split. Child B has toxic epidermal necrolysis: the drug timing, mucosal involvement at two sites, and full thickness gray detachment indicate cytotoxic T cell killing of the whole epidermis, with the fluid loss and sepsis risk of a major burn.

sections.title: Leprosy: how the host response decides the disease

blocks.text: Mycobacterium leprae is an acid fast bacillus with two properties that shape the disease. First, it is an obligate intracellular organism with a massively decayed genome, having lost the genes for many biosynthetic and energy generating pathways, so it depends on the host cell for metabolites and has never been grown in artificial culture; it is propagated in the armadillo or the mouse footpad. Second, it grows optimally at about 30 C (86 F), well below the core temperature of 37 C (98.6 F), so it colonizes the coolest tissues: skin of the face, earlobes, nose, and distal limbs, superficial peripheral nerves such as the ulnar nerve at the elbow, the eye, and the upper respiratory mucosa, while sparing the warm axillae, groin, scalp, and viscera. Within nerves it invades Schwann cells by binding laminin 2 in the basal lamina, which is why sensory loss is an early and defining feature rather than a late complication.

The infection itself has a very long incubation, often 5 to 20 years, and the clinical form is determined almost entirely by the host T cell response rather than by the organism. A vigorous Th1 response, with interleukin 12 driving interferon gamma production, activates macrophages to kill intracellular bacilli and organize them into granulomas, so bacilli are scarce and lesions are few and sharply defined: tuberculoid leprosy presents as one or a few well demarcated, hypopigmented, dry, hairless plaques with raised borders that are strikingly anesthetic to light touch, pinprick, and temperature, together with asymmetric thickening and dysfunction of one or two named nerve trunks. Skin biopsy shows well formed granulomas around nerves with very few or no acid fast bacilli, and the lepromin skin test is positive because cell mediated reactivity is intact.

A Th2 polarized response, with interleukin 4 and interleukin 10 suppressing macrophage activation, fails to kill the organism; bacilli multiply unchecked inside foamy macrophages and are present in enormous numbers. Lepromatous leprosy therefore presents with widespread, poorly demarcated, symmetric infiltrated plaques and nodules, diffuse thickening of facial skin with loss of eyebrows and eyelashes, producing the leonine facies, nasal mucosal involvement with obstruction, epistaxis, and eventual septal collapse (saddle nose), and symmetric glove and stocking peripheral neuropathy from diffuse nerve invasion. Biopsy shows sheets of foamy macrophages packed with acid fast bacilli (lepra cells) and a negative lepromin test. Borderline forms occupy the spectrum between the two poles and are unstable, shifting toward either pole as immunity changes. The neurologic consequences are what disable the patient: anesthetic hands and feet accumulate unnoticed trauma, burns, and ulcers, and motor nerve damage produces claw hand and foot drop, so the deformities of leprosy are largely the result of denervation rather than of direct bacterial destruction.

sections.title: Cutaneous anthrax and the anthrax toxins

blocks.text: Bacillus anthracis is a large, aerobic, nonmotile, spore forming gram positive rod appearing in boxcar shaped chains. Spores persist in soil for decades and infect grazing herbivores, so cutaneous anthrax is classically occupational, in people handling hides, wool, hair, bone meal, or carcasses, and it also follows deliberate release. Spores enter through a cut, are taken up by macrophages, germinate, and the vegetative bacilli multiply locally. Cutaneous disease accounts for roughly 95 percent of naturally occurring anthrax; inhaled spores instead produce hemorrhagic mediastinitis.

Virulence rests on two plasmid encoded systems. The capsule, encoded on pXO2, is made of poly D glutamic acid rather than polysaccharide; because it is a polymer of the D isomer it is poorly immunogenic and resists host enzymes, and its negative charge repels phagocytes, so the organism evades ingestion and opsonization. The toxins, encoded on pXO1, follow the AB model with one shared B subunit and two alternative A subunits. Protective antigen is the B component: it binds the host anthrax toxin receptors, is cleaved by a host protease, oligomerizes into a ring, and that ring is endocytosed and forms a pore through which an A subunit is translocated into the cytosol. Its name reflects the fact that antibody against it is protective and it is the basis of the vaccine; without it neither A subunit can enter a cell.

Edema factor is a calmodulin dependent adenylate cyclase. Inside the cytosol it borrows host calmodulin and converts ATP to cyclic AMP far above physiologic regulation. Unopposed cyclic AMP in endothelium and surrounding cells disturbs ion and water handling and raises vascular permeability, so protein rich fluid pours into the interstitium, producing the massive, nonpitting, strikingly painless gelatinous edema that extends well beyond the lesion and gives the toxin its name; the same rise impairs neutrophil chemotaxis. Lethal factor is a zinc dependent metalloprotease that cleaves and inactivates mitogen activated protein kinase kinases, shutting down MAP kinase signaling in macrophages and dendritic cells. That blocks innate immune activation and cytokine responses, impairs endothelial integrity, and at high doses kills macrophages, and lethal toxin is the principal cause of the shock and death of systemic anthrax.

blocks.text: The cutaneous lesion follows the biology. Two to seven days after inoculation, a small painless, often pruritic papule appears on an exposed site, usually the hand, forearm, face, or neck. It becomes a vesicle that ulcerates centrally, and over several days the base necroses and dries into a depressed, coal black, adherent eschar, which gives the organism its name (anthrakis, Greek for coal). The eschar is surrounded by brawny nonpitting edema and often regional lymphadenopathy. The most useful discriminating feature is that the lesion is painless, because the toxins do not provoke the suppurative, nerve irritating inflammation of an abscess; a tender, purulent, fluctuant lesion is a staphylococcal abscess or ecthyma, not anthrax.

sections.title: Scabies, lice, and bedbugs

blocks.text: Ectoparasitic skin disease is largely an immune response to the parasite rather than injury by it, so the timing and distribution of the itch matter more than seeing the organism. Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei variety hominis, a mite about 0.4 mm long. The fertilized female burrows into the stratum corneum at roughly 2 mm per day, laying two or three eggs daily and leaving feces (scybala) behind her. Only about 10 to 15 mites are present in ordinary scabies, so symptoms cannot be explained by mite burden: the itch is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to mite proteins, eggs, and feces. That is why a first infestation itches only after three to six weeks of sensitization while reinfestation itches within a day or two, and why inflammatory papules and nodules appear at sites where no mite is present.

The distribution follows where the stratum corneum is thin and warm: finger web spaces, flexor wrists, elbows, axillary folds, periumbilical skin, belt line, buttocks, areolae in women, and the penis and scrotum in men, where firm pruritic nodules are characteristic. The head and neck are spared in adults but commonly involved in infants, who also show palmoplantar vesicles and pustules. The pathognomonic lesion is the burrow, a short scaly serpiginous grey line a few millimeters long, and itch is classically worse at night as mite activity rises with skin warmth. Transmission needs about 15 to 20 minutes of skin to skin contact, so cases cluster in households, sexual partners, and long term care facilities; diagnosis is confirmed by scraping a burrow in mineral oil and finding mites, eggs, or scybala.

Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is the same mite in a host whose cell mediated immunity cannot mount the hypersensitivity response: advanced HIV infection, human T lymphotropic virus 1 infection, immunosuppressive therapy, severe malnutrition, or impairment that prevents scratching. Without an effective response the mites multiply into the thousands or millions, producing thick, hyperkeratotic, fissured, warty crusts on the hands, feet, elbows, and scalp with surprisingly little itch, enormous mite counts, and extreme contagiousness, so it is a common source of institutional outbreaks.

blocks.text: Lice are wingless blood feeding insects, and their epidemiology follows where they live between meals. Head lice stay on the scalp and transmit by direct head to head contact or shared headgear; nits are cemented to the hair shaft and cannot be slid off, which distinguishes them from hair casts and dandruff. Pubic lice are transmitted sexually, so their presence warrants evaluation for other sexually transmitted infections. Body lice are the one important vector, because they live in clothing seams rather than on the host and travel with the clothing; they thrive in crowding, cold, and situations where clothes cannot be changed, and their feces scratched into the bite transmit Rickettsia prowazekii (epidemic typhus), Bartonella quintana (trench fever), and Borrelia recurrentis (louse borne relapsing fever). Bedbugs feed at night and retreat to crevices by day, so they are rarely seen on the patient, and they are not known to transmit human disease.

integration.text: The organizing principle across this chapter is anatomy. The level a pathogen reaches determines the lesion, so the lesion names the level. A subcorneal pustule is impetigo, a split in the granular layer means desmoglein 1 has been cleaved by a staphylococcal protease or by a pemphigus foliaceus autoantibody, separation at the dermoepidermal junction with full thickness necrosis means cytotoxic T cells have killed the epidermis, infection of the upper dermis and its lymphatics gives the raised sharp border of erysipelas, infection of the deep dermis and fat gives the fading border of cellulitis, inflammation of the fat septa gives the nonulcerating nodules of erythema nodosum, and spread along the superficial fascia gives pain out of proportion to the skin. Microbiology then explains who gets where: keratinases let dermatophytes occupy only dead keratin, lipid dependence confines Malassezia to sebaceous skin, follicular anatomy admits Staphylococcus aureus, and barrier breaches such as a tinea pedis fissure admit streptococci.

Immunology explains severity, and biochemistry explains the toxins. The same organism produces opposite diseases depending on the host response, most clearly in leprosy, where Th1 polarization gives paucibacillary tuberculoid disease and Th2 polarization gives multibacillary lepromatous disease, and in candidiasis, where an intact interleukin 17 axis confines Candida to a fold and its failure produces chronic mucocutaneous disease. Extensive warts or molluscum reports T cell failure, recurrent furuncles report neutrophil failure, and the pattern of skin infection is therefore a readable immunologic assay. The toxins are enzymes with identifiable substrates: a serine protease cutting desmoglein 1, a phospholipase C hydrolyzing membrane lecithin, metalloproteases cleaving synaptobrevin centrally in tetanus and peripherally in botulism, an adenylate cyclase raising cyclic AMP in anthrax, and superantigens cross-linking major histocompatibility complex class II to the T cell receptor in scarlet fever and toxic shock. Two cautions limit this reasoning: clinical appearance overlaps considerably, so cellulitis is mimicked by stasis dermatitis, contact dermatitis, deep vein thrombosis, and gout, and every per exposure transmission figure and prevalence estimate quoted here is an average that varies with source viral load, region, and host factors.

summary: Depth determines appearance: impetigo is subcorneal, bullous impetigo splits the granular layer, erysipelas is upper dermis with a raised sharp border, cellulitis is deep dermis and fat with a fading border, and necrotizing fasciitis travels the superficial fascia.
Acne needs all four steps: follicular hyperkeratinization, androgen driven sebum, Cutibacterium acnes growth, and inflammation after follicular rupture; comedones do not scar and nodules do.
Candidal rashes occupy moist folds with satellite pustules, irritant diaper dermatitis spares the folds, and persistent mucocutaneous candidiasis points to a Th17 or interleukin 17 defect.

Exfoliative toxin is a serine protease that cleaves desmoglein 1: locally it gives bullous impetigo, in the circulation it gives scalded skin syndrome, and mucosa is spared because desmoglein 3 covers mucosal adhesion.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis is drug triggered cytotoxic T cell killing of the full epidermis with two or more mucosal surfaces involved, which is why it scars and kills while scalded skin syndrome heals in two weeks.
Pain out of proportion to the skin, crepitus, and rapid advance mean necrotizing fasciitis, because fascial spread thromboses the vessels and nerves supplying the overlying skin.

Erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis without vasculitis, so shin nodules are tender but never ulcerate or scar, and the task is to find the trigger: streptococcus, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, endemic fungi, inflammatory bowel disease, or pregnancy.

Impetigo from Streptococcus pyogenes can be followed by glomerulonephritis but not by rheumatic fever, and anti DNase B is the better marker after skin infection because skin lipids inhibit streptolysin O.
mecA on SCCmec encodes PBP2a with low beta-lactam affinity, so resistance covers the whole class; community MRSA carries Panton-Valentine leukocidin and the anterior nares are the reservoir.

Needle stick risk falls roughly tenfold at each step, hepatitis B about 30 percent from an e antigen positive source, hepatitis C about 2 percent, HIV about 0.3 percent, tracking circulating viral titer, and only hepatitis B is vaccine preventable.
